pos: n. pl. (the bones of the mouth; in prophecy the place where God sets His hook in a proud nation)
etymology: Middle English jowe, of uncertain origin. Hebrew lechi, the jaw or cheek — the same word behind Lehi, where Samson took the jawbone of an ass, and malqowach, the jaws that seize.
biblical_def: The jaws in Scripture are where God takes hold. To Pharaoh, the great dragon lying in his rivers: “I will put hooks in thy jaws, and I will cause the fish of thy rivers to stick unto thy scales” (Eze 29:4); and to Gog the same sentence, “I will turn thee back, and put hooks into thy jaws, and I will bring thee forth” (Eze 38:4). Isaiah has “a bridle in the jaws of the people, causing them to err” (Isa 30:28). And in the psalm of the cross the jaws are the sufferer's own: “My strength is dried up like a potsherd; and my tongue cleaveth to my jaws; and thou hast brought me into the dust of death” (Psa 22:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the jaw as the bones of the mouth in which the teeth are fixed, and figuratively the mouth of anything as a place of seizure or devouring.
webster_full: JAW, n. The bones of the mouth in which the teeth are fixed. They are movable, and by their motion the mouth is opened and shut.
JAW, n. The mouth of a thing; as the jaws of a gulf; the jaws of death.
BRIDLE, n. The instrument with which a horse is governed and restrained by a rider.
scriptures: My strength is dried up like a potsherd; and my tongue cleaveth to my jaws; and thou hast brought me into the dust of death.

And his breath, as an overflowing stream, shall reach to the midst of the neck, to sift the nations with the sieve of vanity: and there shall be a bridle in the jaws of the people, causing them to err.
Eze 29:4

But I will put hooks in thy jaws, and I will cause the fish of thy rivers to stick unto thy scales, and I will bring thee up out of the midst of thy rivers, and all the fish of thy rivers shall stick unto thy scales.
Eze 38:4

And I will turn thee back, and put hooks into thy jaws, and I will bring thee forth, and all thine army, horses and horsemen, all of them clothed with all sorts of armour, even a great company with bucklers and shields, all of them handling swords:
corruption_summary: The empires that imagine they move themselves are drawn out by a hook, and the hand in the jaw is God's.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel's hook is the sharpest image in Scripture for the sovereignty of God over nations that never consult Him. Pharaoh says the river is mine and I have made it for myself, and God answers by treating him as a fish. Gog comes down of his own evil will, with an army and a plan, and God says I will turn thee back and put hooks into thy jaws and bring thee forth. Neither king is compelled to sin, and neither escapes being governed. This is the Reformed doctrine of concurrence stated in prophetic pictures: the creature acts freely according to his nature, and the Creator's purpose is not thereby endangered but accomplished.

The corruption to name is the assumption that history is finally the product of human decision, so that the church's hope must rise and fall with the plans of powerful men. Isaiah 40 answers it — the nations are as a drop of a bucket, and are counted as the small dust of the balance. Acts 4 answers it in the hardest case, where Herod and Pilate and the Gentiles and the people of Israel gathered together to do whatever God's hand and counsel determined before to be done. Psalm 22 shows the price at which that determination was carried out, and the jaw that dried up in the dust of death was the Son's.
roots_summary: Hebrew lechi (H3895), jaw, cheek; malqowach (H4455), the jaws that seize; chach (H2397), a hook or ring for the nose or jaw.
roots_lines: Hebrew lechi (H3895) — jaw, cheek bone; Psalm 22:15, Judges 15:15, Isaiah 30:28.
Hebrew malqowach (H4455) — jaws, prey taken; Psalm 22:15, Isaiah 49:24.
Hebrew chach (H2397) — hook, ring, chain; Ezekiel 29:4, 38:4, 2 Kings 19:28.
Hebrew resen (H7448) — bridle, halter; Isaiah 30:28, Job 30:11.
Hebrew cheres (H2789) — potsherd, earthenware; Psalm 22:15, Job 2:8.
usage: “My tongue cleaveth to my jaws” — the thirst of the crucified in Psalm 22.
“I will put hooks in thy jaws” — the LORD to Pharaoh the river dragon.
“A bridle in the jaws of the people” — Isaiah on judicial hardening.

pos: n. (the back of the foot; in Scripture the place of the serpent's wound, of Jacob's grasp, and of the traitor's contempt)
etymology: Old English hela. Hebrew aqeb, the heel, from which comes Yaaqob — Jacob, heel-catcher, supplanter. The name and the wound share a root.
biblical_def: The first promise of the gospel is spoken about a heel: “it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel” (Gen 3:15). The second son of Isaac was named for one: “his hand took hold on Esau's heel; and his name was called Jacob” (Gen 25:26), and Hosea recalls it — “He took his brother by the heel in the womb, and by his strength he had power with God” (Hos 12:3). David gives it its bitterest sense: “mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me” (Psa 41:9), which Christ applied to Judas at the table (Joh 13:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the heel as the hind part of the foot, and notes the scriptural phrase of lifting up the heel as an act of contempt or treachery.
webster_full: HEEL, n. The hind part of the foot, particularly of man; the projecting extremity of the foot behind.
HEEL, n. To lift up the heel against, in Scripture, is to treat with insolence, or to spurn and act treacherously toward.
SUPPLANT, v.t. To trip up the heels; hence, to displace by stratagem, or to displace and take the place of.
scriptures: Gen 3:15
And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel.
And after that came his brother out, and his hand took hold on Esau's heel; and his name was called Jacob: and Isaac was threescore years old when she bare them.
Psa 41:9
Yea, mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me.
And the God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. Amen.
corruption_summary: Genesis 3:15 sets two wounds side by side and they are not equal — a crushed head against a bruised heel.
corruption_paragraphs: The protevangelium is the whole gospel in a sentence, and its power is in the asymmetry. The serpent strikes the heel; the seed of the woman crushes the head. One wound is real and grievous and temporary — the cross, the grave, the three days. The other is mortal. The Reformers read this verse as the first preaching of Christ, and the whole Bible after it is the working out of the enmity God Himself put between the two seeds. Romans 16:20 hands the promise to the church: the God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly, which is to say the victory of the Head is shared with the body.

The corruption to name is the reduction of Genesis 3:15 to a moral fable about human beings overcoming their difficulties, and the parallel error of treating Satan as a symbol of impersonal forces. Scripture is not vague here. There is a serpent, he is called the devil and Satan in Revelation 12:9, and the enmity is a matter of divine appointment rather than human choice. Equally to be resisted is the opposite excess that gives the enemy a dignity Scripture never grants him — a defeated creature on a chain, whose head was crushed at Calvary and whose sentence is already written.
roots_summary: Hebrew aqeb (H6119), heel, footprint; aqab (H6117), to supplant, take by the heel; shuph (H7779), to bruise or crush.
roots_lines: Hebrew aqeb (H6119) — heel, footprint; Genesis 3:15, 25:26, Psalm 41:9.
Hebrew aqab (H6117) — to supplant, take by the heel; Genesis 27:36, Hosea 12:3.
Hebrew shuph (H7779) — to bruise, crush; Genesis 3:15 twice, Job 9:17.
Greek pterna (G4418) — heel; John 13:18 only.
Greek suntribo (G4937) — to break, bruise; Romans 16:20, Luke 9:39.
usage: “It shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel” — the first gospel promise.
“His hand took hold on Esau's heel” — and his name was called Jacob.
“Hath lifted up his heel against me” — David of his friend, Christ of Judas.

pos: n. pl. (the sides of the body between ribs and hip; in Leviticus the location of the fat reserved to the LORD)
etymology: Old French flanc, the side. Hebrew kesel, the loins or flanks — and by a striking extension the same consonants carry the sense of confidence, since the loins were the seat of a man's strength.
biblical_def: The flanks appear in Scripture almost entirely in one repeated formula of the offerings. Of the peace offering: “the two kidneys, and the fat that is on them, which is by the flanks, and the caul above the liver, with the kidneys, it shall he take away” (Lev 3:4), and the same words again of the lamb (Lev 3:10) and the goat (Lev 3:15) and the sin offering (Lev 4:9). The reason the formula is repeated without variation is given at the end of the chapter: “the priest shall burn them upon the altar: it is the food of the offering made by fire for a sweet savour: all the fat is the LORD'S” (Lev 3:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the flank as the fleshy or muscular part of the side of an animal, between the ribs and the hip.
webster_full: FLANK, n. The fleshy or muscular part of the side of an animal, between the ribs and the hip.
CAUL, n. A little membrane covering the lower intestines; the omentum.
KIDNEY, n. The kidneys are two oblong flattened bodies, situated in the loins, whose office is to separate the urine from the blood.
scriptures: Lev 3:4
And the two kidneys, and the fat that is on them, which is by the flanks, and the caul above the liver, with the kidneys, it shall he take away.
Lev 3:10
And the two kidneys, and the fat that is upon them, which is by the flanks, and the caul above the liver, with the kidneys, it shall he take away.
Lev 3:15
And the two kidneys, and the fat that is upon them, which is by the flanks, and the caul above the liver, with the kidneys, it shall he take away.
Lev 3:16
And the priest shall burn them upon the altar: it is the food of the offering made by fire for a sweet savour: all the fat is the LORD'S.
corruption_summary: The inward fat was burnt to God and never eaten, which taught Israel that the best and the hidden parts belong to Him first.
corruption_paragraphs: Leviticus 3 repeats its inventory four times without a word changed, and the repetition is the lesson. The fat about the kidneys and the flanks was the richest portion of the animal, deep inside where no worshipper could see it, and it went entirely to the fire. Israel ate the peace offering — it was the one sacrifice the offerer shared — but not that. All the fat is the LORD'S. What was hidden and what was best were His by statute, and the same chapter forbids the eating of blood in the same breath, joining the two prohibitions that guarded the altar.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God claims the inward and the excellent, not the surplus and the visible. Malachi 1 is the standing rebuke of the reverse practice — offering the blind, the lame, and the sick, and the LORD asking whether the governor would accept it. Romans 12 carries the principle into the New Covenant without the altar: present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service. The fat by the flanks is a small ceremonial detail teaching a large and permanent thing.
roots_summary: Hebrew kesel (H3689), flank, loins, and confidence; cheleb (H2459), fat, the best of a thing; yothereth (H3508), the caul above the liver.
roots_lines: Hebrew kesel (H3689) — flank, loins, confidence; Leviticus 3:4, Job 15:27, Psalm 78:7.
Hebrew cheleb (H2459) — fat, the choicest part; Leviticus 3:16, Genesis 45:18.
Hebrew yothereth (H3508) — the caul, lobe of the liver; Leviticus 3:4, 9:10.
Hebrew kilyah (H3629) — kidneys, reins, the inward parts; Leviticus 3:4, Psalm 16:7.
Hebrew reyach nichoach — a sweet savour; Leviticus 3:16, Genesis 8:21.
usage: “The fat that is on them, which is by the flanks” — repeated without variation four times.
“All the fat is the LORD'S” — the reason for the repetition.
The hidden and the best, burnt where no worshipper could see it.

pos: adj. (unable to speak; in the parables and in Acts, the silence of a man with nothing to say for himself)
etymology: English speech + -less. The Greek of Matthew 22 is phimoo, to be muzzled — the same verb Christ used to still the sea and to silence the unclean spirit.
biblical_def: Three silences. At the wedding the king finds a man without a garment: “Friend, how camest thou in hither not having a wedding garment? And he was speechless” (Mat 22:12), and the sentence follows at once (Mat 22:13). Zacharias, who had doubted Gabriel, “could not speak unto them… for he beckoned unto them, and remained speechless” (Luk 1:22), having been told, “thou shalt be dumb, and not able to speak… because thou believest not my words” (Luk 1:20). And on the Damascus road, “the men which journeyed with him stood speechless, hearing a voice, but seeing no man” (Act 9:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines speechless as destitute or deprived of the power of speaking, and also as mute or silent, not speaking for a time.
webster_full: SPEECHLESS, a. Destitute or deprived of the faculty of speech.
SPEECHLESS, a. Mute; silent; not speaking for a time.
MUZZLE, v.t. To bind the mouth; to fasten the mouth to prevent biting or eating.
scriptures: And he saith unto him, Friend, how camest thou in hither not having a wedding garment? And he was speechless.
Then said the king to the servants, Bind him hand and foot, and take him away, and cast him into outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
Luk 1:20
And, behold, thou shalt be dumb, and not able to speak, until the day that these things shall be performed, because thou believest not my words, which shall be fulfilled in their season.
Rom 3:19
Now we know that what things soever the law saith, it saith to them who are under the law: that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God.
corruption_summary: The man without the wedding garment had no answer, and Scripture makes that silence the posture of every sinner before the law.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 22:12 and Romans 3:19 are the same doctrine in two keys. The guest is inside the hall, seated, apparently accepted, and one question undoes him: how camest thou in hither not having a wedding garment? He was speechless — muzzled, the Greek says, the word used of the silenced sea. Paul states the principle: the law speaks that every mouth may be stopped and all the world become guilty before God. Justification cannot begin until the excuses end, and the whole doctrine of imputed righteousness stands on the fact that the garment is provided rather than produced. He was not cast out for lacking merit; he was cast out for coming in his own.

The corruption to name is the confidence that a reasonable account of oneself will be accepted at the last. It is the working assumption of most religion and of most irreligion — that when the question comes, something can be said: sincerity, decency, intention, comparison with worse men. The parable removes the option. And notice the address: the king calls him Friend, the same word Christ used to Judas in the garden. Nearness is not safety, and a place at the table is not a garment.
roots_summary: Greek phimoo (G5392), to muzzle, put to silence; siopao (G4623), to be silent; eneos (G1769), speechless, dumb with amazement.
roots_lines: Greek phimoo (G5392) — to muzzle, silence; Matthew 22:12, Mark 4:39, 1 Timothy 5:18.
Greek eneos (G1769) — speechless, dumb; Acts 9:7 only.
Greek siopao (G4623) — to be silent, hold one's peace; Luke 1:20, Mark 14:61.
Greek phrasso (G5420) — to stop, close the mouth; Romans 3:19, 2 Corinthians 11:10.
Greek hupodikos (G5267) — guilty, answerable to; Romans 3:19 only.
usage: “And he was speechless” — the guest without a wedding garment.
“Thou shalt be dumb… because thou believest not my words” — Gabriel to Zacharias.
“That every mouth may be stopped” — the law's purpose, in Paul's words.

pos: adj. (having the hair whitened with age; in Scripture a mark for honour and a call to testify)
etymology: English gray + head. The Hebrew is sib or sebah, hoariness — and the law attaches a commandment to it, requiring the young to rise before the hoary head.
biblical_def: Samuel steps down grayheaded and appeals to the record: “I am old and grayheaded; and, behold, my sons are with you: and I have walked before you from my childhood unto this day” (1Sa 12:2). Eliphaz claims the advantage of years against Job: “With us are both the grayheaded and very aged men, much elder than thy father” (Job 15:10). And the psalmist prays the one prayer proper to old age: “Now also when I am old and grayheaded, O God, forsake me not; until I have shewed thy strength unto this generation, and thy power to every one that is to come” (Psa 71:18). The law had already commanded the honour: “Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man, and fear thy God” (Lev 19:32).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines grayheaded as having gray hair, and gray as white with a mixture of black, the color of the hair in old age.
webster_full: GRAYHEADED, a. Having gray hair; hoary.
GRAY, a. White with a mixture of black; hoary; as gray hairs.
HOARY, a. White or whitish; white or gray with age; as hoary hairs; a hoary head.
scriptures: And now, behold, the king walketh before you: and I am old and grayheaded; and, behold, my sons are with you: and I have walked before you from my childhood unto this day.
With us are both the grayheaded and very aged men, much elder than thy father.
Now also when I am old and grayheaded, O God, forsake me not; until I have shewed thy strength unto this generation, and thy power to every one that is to come.
Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man, and fear thy God: I am the LORD.
corruption_summary: Age is commanded honour and is not by itself wisdom, and Job 15 shows the difference by putting the claim in the mouth of a man who was wrong.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture holds two things about the grayhead without embarrassment. The first is that honour is owed: rise up before the hoary head, and fear thy God — the command grounded not in the old man's merit but in the fear of the LORD, which is why it is not negotiable when the old man is difficult. The second is that years do not guarantee understanding. Eliphaz plays the grayheaded card against Job and is rebuked by God in chapter 42; Elihu, the youngest in the room, says plainly that great men are not always wise. Proverbs settles it: the hoary head is a crown of glory if it be found in the way of righteousness. The condition is in the text.

The corruption to name is a culture that has abolished both halves. It does not rise before the hoary head — age is treated as obsolescence, and the old are moved out of sight and out of counsel. And where it does honour age, it often honours it uncritically, as though experience were self-authenticating. Psalm 71 shows the fitting ambition of the aged saint, and it is not comfort but testimony: forsake me not, until I have shewed thy strength unto this generation. The grayhead in Scripture is not retiring. He is still talking about God to the young.
roots_summary: Hebrew sib (H7867), to be gray-haired; sebah (H7872), hoary head, old age; zaqen (H2205), old man, elder.
roots_lines: Hebrew sib (H7867) — to be grayheaded; 1 Samuel 12:2, Job 15:10.
Hebrew sebah (H7872) — hoary head, gray hair, old age; Leviticus 19:32, Proverbs 16:31, Isaiah 46:4.
Hebrew zaqen (H2205) — old man, elder; Leviticus 19:32, Deuteronomy 32:7.
Hebrew dor (H1755) — generation; Psalm 71:18, Psalm 145:4.
Hebrew zeroa (H2220) — arm, strength; Psalm 71:18, Isaiah 53:1.
usage: “I am old and grayheaded” — Samuel's farewell to Israel.
“O God, forsake me not; until I have shewed thy strength unto this generation.”
“Rise up before the hoary head” — the honour the law commands.

pos: adj. (thin, wasted; of the seven kine of Pharaoh's dream that devoured the fat and were no better for it)
etymology: English lean + flesh, rendering Hebrew daq basar, thin of flesh. The word occurs once, and the picture it draws governs seven years of history and the whole career of Joseph.
biblical_def: “And the ill favoured and leanfleshed kine did eat up the seven well favoured and fat kine. So Pharaoh awoke” (Gen 41:4). The dream troubled him because the eating changed nothing — “the lean and the ill favoured kine did eat up the first seven fat kine” (Gen 41:20), and they were as bad as at the beginning. Joseph read it: “the seven thin and ill favoured kine that came up after them are seven years; and the seven empty ears blasted with the east wind shall be seven years of famine” (Gen 41:27). Behind the whole of it was a purpose Joseph named later — God sent him before them to preserve life.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lean as wanting flesh, meager, thin, and by extension barren or unproductive; leanfleshed is thin in body.
webster_full: LEAN, a. Wanting flesh; meager; not fat; as a lean body; a lean man or animal.
LEAN, a. Barren; not fertile or productive; as a lean soil.
LEANNESS, n. Destitution of flesh, or of fat; thinness of body; meagerness.
scriptures: Gen 41:4
And the ill favoured and leanfleshed kine did eat up the seven well favoured and fat kine. So Pharaoh awoke.
And the lean and the ill favoured kine did eat up the first seven fat kine:
And the seven thin and ill favoured kine that came up after them are seven years; and the seven empty ears blasted with the east wind shall be seven years of famine.
Job 9:10
Which doeth great things past finding out; yea, and wonders without number.
corruption_summary: A pagan king dreams and the God of Israel is the one speaking, and the whole of Genesis 41 turns on Joseph's refusal to take credit for the interpretation.
corruption_paragraphs: Pharaoh dreams, and God is the dreamer's author. Joseph says so before he says anything else: it is not in me; God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace. That single sentence is the reason the chapter ends with Joseph over all the land of Egypt. Scripture is quite willing to record God speaking into a heathen court — to Pharaoh here, to Nebuchadnezzar in Daniel 2, to Abimelech in Genesis 20 — and never suggests that the recipients were therefore godly. The revelation is a mercy to many and a conversion to none of them by itself.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sufficiency of God's providential government over famine and plenty alike. The lean kine ate the fat and remained lean: the sober warning that stored abundance can be swallowed without a trace, which is precisely what makes Joseph's twenty-percent granary policy an act of faith rather than mere prudence. Seven good years are not a promise of an eighth. The believer's security is never in the fat years he has banked but in the God who sent both the plenty and the famine, and who sent a man ahead into Egypt to preserve a posterity in the earth.
roots_summary: Hebrew daq (H1851), thin, small, lean; basar (H1320), flesh; raab (H7458), famine, hunger.
roots_lines: Hebrew daq (H1851) — thin, lean, small; Genesis 41:3, 41:4, Leviticus 16:12.
Hebrew basar (H1320) — flesh, body; Genesis 41:2, Isaiah 40:6.
Hebrew raab (H7458) — famine, hunger; Genesis 41:27, 41:54, Amos 8:11.
Hebrew chalom (H2472) — dream; Genesis 41:7, 37:5, Daniel 2:1.
Hebrew qadim (H6921) — east wind; Genesis 41:27, Exodus 14:21.
usage: “The ill favoured and leanfleshed kine did eat up the… fat kine” — and were no better.
“Seven thin and ill favoured kine… are seven years” — Joseph's reading.
“So Pharaoh awoke” — a heathen king troubled by the God of Israel.

pos: n. pl. (the newly born and very young; in Scripture objects of Christ's welcome and of war's worst cruelty)
etymology: Latin infans, not speaking, from in- + fari, to speak. The Greek of Luke 18 is brephos, a babe in arms or unborn — the same word used of John leaping in Elisabeth's womb.
biblical_def: Job wishes he had been “as infants which never saw light” (Job 3:16). Hosea records the atrocity Samaria had earned: “their infants shall be dashed in pieces, and their women with child shall be ripped up” (Hos 13:16). And Luke sets against both the scene at which the disciples took offence: “they brought unto him also infants, that he would touch them: but when his disciples saw it, they rebuked them” (Luk 18:15) — and the Lord overruled them, “Suffer little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God” (Luk 18:16). The word Luke uses for these infants is the word he used of the unborn Baptist.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an infant as a child in the first period of life, and in law a person under the age of full legal capacity, entitled to particular protection.
webster_full: INFANT, n. A child in the first period of life, beginning at his birth; a young babe.
INFANT, n. In law, a person under the age of twenty one years, who is incapable of making a valid contract.
INFANTILE, a. Pertaining to infancy, or to an infant.
scriptures: Job 3:16
Or as an hidden untimely birth I had not been; as infants which never saw light.
Samaria shall become desolate; for she hath rebelled against her God: they shall fall by the sword: their infants shall be dashed in pieces, and their women with child shall be ripped up.
And they brought unto him also infants, that he would touch them: but when his disciples saw it, they rebuked them.
But Jesus called them unto him, and said, Suffer little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God.
corruption_summary: Luke uses the same word for the infants in arms and for the unborn John, and the child in the womb is therefore not a candidate for personhood but a person.
corruption_paragraphs: The vocabulary is decisive. Luke 1:41 says the brephos leaped in Elisabeth's womb; Luke 2:12 says the brephos lay in the manger; Luke 18:15 says they brought unto Him the brephos. One word covers the unborn, the newborn, and the babe in arms, because Scripture recognizes no boundary between them. Psalm 139 says the same in the language of worship — thou hast covered me in my mother's womb; mine substance was not hid from thee. Jeremiah 1:5 says it in the language of calling. The child in the womb is a human being made in the image of God, known by name before birth.

The corruption to name is the doctrine that personhood is conferred by development, viability, or the wishes of others, which is the argumentative core of abortion in every form it takes. It is not a new error but an ancient one wearing modern language: the exposure of unwanted infants was ordinary in the Greco-Roman world the church was born into, and the church opposed it from the beginning. Hosea 13:16 names the killing of infants as the extremity of judgment and horror, not as a private matter. And the answer of Christ to disciples who thought children beneath His time is the answer still: suffer them to come, and forbid them not.
roots_summary: Greek brephos (G1025), an unborn child, newborn, or babe in arms; paidion (G3813), little child; Hebrew olel (H5768), infant, suckling.
roots_lines: Greek brephos (G1025) — unborn child, babe; Luke 1:41, 2:12, 18:15, Acts 7:19.
Greek paidion (G3813) — little child; Luke 18:16, Matthew 18:2.
Hebrew olel (H5768) — infant, suckling; Hosea 13:16, Psalm 8:2, Lamentations 2:11.
Hebrew nephel (H5309) — untimely birth; Job 3:16, Ecclesiastes 6:3.
Hebrew yatsar (H3335) — to form, fashion; Jeremiah 1:5, Psalm 139:16.
usage: “They brought unto him also infants, that he would touch them” — and the disciples rebuked them.
“Of such is the kingdom of God” — the Lord's correction.
“As infants which never saw light” — Job in the depth of his grief.

pos: n. (a woman who attends a birth; in Exodus, the first recorded civil disobedience in Scripture)
etymology: Middle English mid, with, + wif, woman — she who is with the woman. Hebrew yalad in its causative form, one who helps to bring forth.
biblical_def: The midwife speaks comfort at Rachel's death: “when she was in hard labour, that the midwife said unto her, Fear not; thou shalt have this son also” (Gen 35:17). She marks the firstborn of Tamar's twins with a scarlet thread (Gen 38:28). And in Exodus she is given a command she refuses: “When ye do the office of a midwife to the Hebrew women… if it be a son, then ye shall kill him” (Exo 1:16). Shiphrah and Puah would not. “But the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men children alive” (Exo 1:17), and God dealt well with them and made them houses.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a midwife as a woman who assists other women in childbirth, and midwifery as the art or practice of assisting women in parturition.
webster_full: MIDWIFE, n. A woman who assists other women in childbirth.
MIDWIFERY, n. The art or practice of assisting women in childbirth; obstetrics.
PARTURITION, n. The act of bringing forth young.
scriptures: And it came to pass, when she was in hard labour, that the midwife said unto her, Fear not; thou shalt have this son also.
And it came to pass, when she travailed, that the one put out his hand: and the midwife took and bound upon his hand a scarlet thread, saying, This came out first.
Exo 1:16
And he said, When ye do the office of a midwife to the Hebrew women, and see them upon the stools; if it be a son, then ye shall kill him: but if it be a daughter, then she shall live.
Exo 1:17
But the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men children alive.
corruption_summary: Shiphrah and Puah disobeyed a king to obey God, and Scripture records the reason in five words: the midwives feared God.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 1 is the Bible's founding case on the limits of civil authority. Pharaoh held every lawful title to rule and issued a command within his jurisdiction, and two women refused it, because the state had ordered them to commit murder. The text gives the whole rationale in one clause — the midwives feared God — and then records that God dealt well with them and made them houses. Peter and John in Acts 4 state the principle: whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye. The Reformed tradition has always held both halves: the magistrate is God's minister and is to be obeyed, and his authority is delegated and therefore bounded.

The corruption to name is at both edges. On one side is the doctrine that the state's command is finally the highest, so that a lawful order settles the conscience — the defence that failed at Nuremberg and fails in Exodus 1. On the other is the modern reflex that treats any disliked law as a matter for conscience, which empties the category by inflating it. Romans 13 is not repealed by Exodus 1. The midwives disobeyed one specific command to kill and went on living under Pharaoh, and their names were written into Scripture while his was not.
roots_summary: Hebrew yalad (H3205), to bear, bring forth, act as midwife; obnayim (H70), the birthstool; yare (H3372), to fear, reverence.
roots_lines: Hebrew yalad (H3205) — to bring forth, act as midwife; Genesis 35:17, Exodus 1:16.
Hebrew obnayim (H70) — birthstool, potter's wheel; Exodus 1:16, Jeremiah 18:3.
Hebrew yare (H3372) — to fear, reverence; Exodus 1:17, 1:21, Proverbs 1:7.
Hebrew bayith (H1004) — house, household; Exodus 1:21, 2 Samuel 7:11.
Hebrew shani (H8144) — scarlet, crimson thread; Genesis 38:28, Joshua 2:18.
usage: “Fear not; thou shalt have this son also” — the midwife to dying Rachel.
“If it be a son, then ye shall kill him” — Pharaoh's order.
“But the midwives feared God” — and did not as the king commanded.

pos: n. pl. (two born at one birth; in Genesis the setting for the doctrine of election)
etymology: Old English getwinn, twofold. Hebrew teom, a twin — the root behind the name Thomas, called Didymus, the twin.
biblical_def: Twins are born twice in Genesis and both times the birth carries doctrine. Of Rebekah: “when her days to be delivered were fulfilled, behold, there were twins in her womb” (Gen 25:24), of whom the LORD had already said, “Two nations are in thy womb… and the elder shall serve the younger” (Gen 25:23). Of Tamar: “in the time of her travail, that, behold, twins were in her womb” (Gen 38:27). The Song uses the word for beauty and abundance — teeth like a flock “whereof every one bear twins, and none is barren among them” (Son 4:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a twin as one of two young produced at a birth by an animal that ordinarily brings forth but one, and as an adjective, born at the same birth.
webster_full: TWIN, n. One of two young produced at a birth by an animal that usually brings forth but one.
TWIN, a. Noting two born at a birth; as twin brothers.
TWIN, a. Very much resembling; as twin virtues.
scriptures: And the LORD said unto her, Two nations are in thy womb, and two manner of people shall be separated from thy bowels; and the one people shall be stronger than the other people; and the elder shall serve the younger.
And when her days to be delivered were fulfilled, behold, there were twins in her womb.
And it came to pass in the time of her travail, that, behold, twins were in her womb.
Son 4:2
Thy teeth are like a flock of sheep that are even shorn, which came up from the washing; whereof every one bear twins, and none is barren among them.
corruption_summary: Paul builds unconditional election on twins in one womb, because nothing but the purpose of God could distinguish them.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 9 chooses this example on purpose. Jacob and Esau shared a father, a mother, a womb, and a birthday; and God said the elder shall serve the younger before they were born, neither having done any good or evil. Paul draws the conclusion himself: that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him that calleth. Every ground of distinction that men reach for is removed by the circumstances of the case. If God's choice rested on foreseen faith, foreseen works, or foreseen anything, Genesis 25:23 was spoken too early. Unconditional election is not a doctrine imposed on this text; it is the reason the text is written the way it is.

The corruption to name is the reading that makes Romans 9 about nations rather than persons, so that election becomes a matter of historical roles and not of salvation. Paul will not permit the escape: he moves from Jacob and Esau to Pharaoh to vessels of mercy prepared unto glory, and answers the objection any honest reader raises — why doth he yet find fault? — not by softening the doctrine but by asking who the objector is. The corporate reading is offered as a kindness to God's reputation. God does not need it, and Paul does not use it.
roots_summary: Hebrew teom (H8380), twin; Greek Didumos (G1324), Didymus, the twin; Greek ekloge (G1589), election, choosing out.
roots_lines: Hebrew teom (H8380) — twin; Genesis 25:24, 38:27, Song of Solomon 4:2.
Greek Didumos (G1324) — Didymus, twin; John 11:16, 20:24, 21:2.
Greek ekloge (G1589) — election, the act of choosing; Romans 9:11, 11:5, 2 Peter 1:10.
Hebrew rab / tsair — the elder, the younger; Genesis 25:23.
Hebrew beten (H990) — belly, womb; Genesis 25:23, Psalm 139:13.
usage: “Behold, there were twins in her womb” — Rebekah delivered.
“The elder shall serve the younger” — spoken before they were born.
“Every one bear twins, and none is barren” — the Song's figure of fruitfulness.

pos: v. (drew a deep and grieving breath; used of Israel under bondage and of Christ before healing)
etymology: Old English sican. Hebrew anach, to groan; the Greek of Mark is stenazo and anastenazo — to groan up out of the depths, the same root Paul uses of the whole creation groaning.
biblical_def: Israel in Egypt: “the children of Israel sighed by reason of the bondage, and they cried, and their cry came up unto God” (Exo 2:23), and the next verse gives the ground of the whole exodus — “God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob” (Exo 2:24). Twice Mark records the sighing of Christ. Before opening the ears of the deaf man: “looking up to heaven, he sighed, and saith unto him, Ephphatha, that is, Be opened” (Mar 7:34). And before the Pharisees who came demanding a sign: “he sighed deeply in his spirit, and saith, Why doth this generation seek after a sign?” (Mar 8:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to sigh as to inhale a larger quantity of air than usual and emit it, as under grief or oppression of mind, and a sigh as a single deep respiration expressing sorrow.
webster_full: SIGH, v.i. To inhale a larger quantity of air than usual, and immediately expel it; to suffer a deep single respiration.
SIGH, n. A single deep respiration; a long breath; the inhaling of a larger quantity of air than usual, and the sudden emission of it, occasioned by grief.
GROAN, v.i. To breathe with a deep murmuring sound; to utter a mournful voice, as in pain or sorrow.
scriptures: Exo 2:23

And it came to pass in process of time, that the king of Egypt died: and the children of Israel sighed by reason of the bondage, and they cried, and their cry came up unto God by reason of the bondage.
Exo 2:24
And God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob.
Mar 7:34
And looking up to heaven, he sighed, and saith unto him, Ephphatha, that is, Be opened.
Mar 8:12
And he sighed deeply in his spirit, and saith, Why doth this generation seek after a sign? verily I say unto you, There shall no sign be given unto this generation.
corruption_summary: The Son of God sighed before He healed, which forbids any account of His miracles as effortless display.
corruption_paragraphs: Mark 7 gives a detail no invented account would include. Before the deaf man's ears are opened, Christ takes him aside from the multitude, touches his tongue, looks up to heaven, and sighs. The power is unquestioned; the grief is real. He is standing in a world broken by sin, in front of one man carrying a piece of the ruin, and He groans over it before He undoes it. The same verb belongs to the whole creation in Romans 8, groaning and travailing together until now, and to believers who groan within themselves waiting for the redemption of the body. Christ's sigh joins Him to that groaning without any suggestion that He shares its guilt.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the reality of Christ's human affections against every account that makes them a performance. The impassibility of God is confessed by the Reformed tradition of the divine nature, which does not suffer or change; and the same tradition confesses that in the incarnation the Son took a true human soul with true human emotion, so that He wept at Lazarus' grave, was moved with compassion, and sighed deeply in His spirit. Exodus 2:24 supplies the other half of the comfort: God hears sighing and answers it, not out of sentiment but because He remembers His covenant.
roots_summary: Hebrew anach (H584), to sigh, groan; neaqah (H5009), groaning; Greek stenazo (G4727) and anastenazo (G389), to groan deeply.
roots_lines: Hebrew anach (H584) — to sigh, groan; Exodus 2:23, Ezekiel 9:4, Lamentations 1:8.
Hebrew neaqah (H5009) — groaning; Exodus 2:24, 6:5, Judges 2:18.
Greek stenazo (G4727) — to groan, sigh; Mark 7:34, Romans 8:23, 2 Corinthians 5:2.
Greek anastenazo (G389) — to sigh deeply; Mark 8:12 only.
Hebrew zakar (H2142) — to remember; Exodus 2:24, Genesis 8:1, Psalm 105:8.
usage: “The children of Israel sighed by reason of the bondage” — and their cry came up unto God.
“He sighed, and saith unto him, Ephphatha” — grief before healing.
“He sighed deeply in his spirit” — at a generation demanding a sign.
